label: The Absolute Encodes the Metric
notes: Open by reframing the whole chapter: Euclidean geometry is projective geometry that fixes one extra datum, the pair of circular points I and J at infinity. Everything metric, angle, distance, orthogonality, circles, follows from how a figure relates to that invisible pair. Stress that I and J are ordinary complex projective points we will compute with.

label: The Circular Points I and J
notes: Define the circular points as the complex intersections of every circle with the line at infinity. Write their coordinates and emphasize they are conjugate. The pair is what an affine transformation may move but a similarity must fix; that invariance is exactly why they carry Euclidean structure. Tell students to treat them as legitimate points over C.

label: Isotropic Lines and Degenerate Length
notes: Introduce isotropic, or minimal, lines as the lines joining a finite point to I or J. Along them the quadratic form measuring squared length vanishes, so Euclidean distance degenerates to zero. This is the metric singularity hidden inside the absolute. Connect it to why these lines are invisible in any real drawing yet decisive algebraically.

label: Laguerre's Angle Formula
notes: Present Laguerre's formula as the centerpiece: the angle between two real lines is a logarithm of the cross ratio that their infinite points form with I and J. Walk through why a multiplicative cross ratio becomes an additive angle through the logarithm, and why the factor one over two i normalizes it. This is angle as pure incidence data.

label: Bracket Construction of Bisectors
notes: Show the angle bisector emerging directly from brackets involving I and J. The square-root combination of the four brackets gives lambda and mu, and the points lambda I plus or minus mu J are the two infinite directions of the internal and external bisectors. Note they come out automatically perpendicular, recovering a classical fact from pure algebra.

label: Distance up to a Similarity Factor
notes: Explain the analogue for distance: the same circular-point brackets recover Euclidean length, but only up to an overall scale because similarities, which rescale distance, are exactly the maps fixing I and J. Contrast this with angle, which is absolutely determined. The unfixable factor is the projective fingerprint of similarity invariance.

label: Euclidean Maps Fix the Pair {I,J}
notes: State the group-theoretic punchline: the projectivities that fix the unordered pair I, J are precisely the similarities. Fixing each point separately gives orientation-preserving maps; swapping them adds reflections and conjugation. Translations and rotations sit inside as the subgroup also fixing the line at infinity pointwise structure. This is the cleanest definition of Euclidean motion available.

label: Circles Pass Through I and J
notes: Define a circle projectively as any conic through both circular points. Then the center is the meet of the two complex tangents drawn at I and J, a real point even though the tangents are complex. Emphasize the diagram shows the real consequence of a complex construction, and that this characterizes circles among all conics.

label: Foci from Tangents Through I and J
notes: Generalize the circle center idea to arbitrary conics: draw the complex tangents from I and from J, and their intersections are the foci. For a real ellipse exactly two of the four pairings are real, matching the classical foci. This unifies center and focus as one circular-point construction and explains the reflection law of conics.

label: Mirror Image as Seven Joins and Meets
notes: Reconstruct reflection projectively: join the point to I and J, meet those lines with the mirror, then cross-join with J and I. Seven incidence operations reproduce the ordinary reflection, with the midpoint landing on the mirror and the segment perpendicular to it. Highlight that a SymPy check confirms the identity exactly for the horizontal mirror.

label: Triangle Theorems as Incidence
notes: Frame classical triangle centers as a translation test. Medians need only harmonic midpoints, no metric. Altitudes and bisectors additionally invoke the circular-point metric for orthogonality. The Euler line then appears as a collinearity statement. The lesson: sorting each hypothesis into affine, projective, or genuinely metric clarifies what the absolute actually contributes.

label: Nine-Point Circle Relaxes to a Conic
notes: Close with the hybrid lab. Drop the hypothesis that H is the orthocenter; the six midpoints and three cevian feet still lie on a conic, which becomes the nine-point circle only when the metric condition is restored. Recap the chapter thesis: the absolute pair I, J is the single projective object that encodes all Euclidean measurement.
